extracted.intended_audience: the people of the State of New York; informed citizens and policymakers debating the proposed Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of the proper structure, powers, and relations of the national judiciary under the proposed U.S. Constitution, addressing original vs appellate jurisdiction, relation to state courts, and practical safeguards. Written as guidance/argument for citizens evaluating the Constitution's judiciary provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileges and immunities enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The citizens of each State shall be entitled to all the privileges and immunities of citizens of the several States; to secure the full effect of so fundamental a provision against all evasion and subterfuge, its construction should be committed to that tribunal which, having no local attachments, will be likely to be impartial between the different States and their citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because equality of privileges/immunities must be inviolably maintained, national judiciary ought to preside in cases where one State or its citizens are opposed to another State or its citizens to prevent evasion by local bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality via national tribunal without local attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: The national judiciary, owing its official existence to the Union and having no local attachments, will be likely to be impartial between the different States and their citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commit construction of fundamental national provisions to a tribunal detached from local interests to avoid bias; local courts may have prejudices tied to their State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal cognizance of maritime causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The national judiciary has cognizance of maritime causes; these generally depend on the laws of nations and commonly affect the rights of foreigners, falling within considerations relative to the public peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maritime/admiralty jurisdiction is naturally federal because of international law connections and foreign interests; most such causes are already submitted to federal jurisdiction under the Confederation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power over cases in law and equity arising under Constitution/laws/treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend to all cases in law and equity, arising under the Constitution, the laws of the United States, and treaties made, or which shall be made, under their authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes controversies that result directly from constitutional restrictions on states (e.g., prohibitions on emitting paper money) as 'cases arising under the Constitution' distinct from those arising under federal statutes; 'equity' included because many litigated subjects may involve fraud, accident, trust, or hardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable jurisdiction necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity jurisdiction is necessary because many subjects of litigation involve ingredients of FRAUD, ACCIDENT, TRUST, or HARDSHIP which render matters objects of equitable rather than legal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: relief against hard bargains, agreements to convey lands claimed under grants of different States; equitable remedies are required especially when foreigners are concerned and to do justice where legal forms may not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power over treaties and diplomatic cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend to treaties made, or which shall be made, under the authority of the United States, and to all cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These belong to the class of causes connected with the preservation of the national peace and respect to sovereignties represented by public ministers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiralty and maritime jurisdiction as federal
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary authority of the Union is to extend to cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reiterates maritime causes as proper subjects for national courts because of their international aspects and need for uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversies to which the United States shall be a party
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts extend to controversies to which the United States shall be a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the national government is a party, federal cognizance is naturally appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-state controversies jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction extends to controversies between two or more States; between a State and citizens of another State; between citizens of different States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These classes of causes implicate the relations between States and citizens across State lines and thus fall under national judicial authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disputes between citizens of same State over land under different State grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases between the citizens of the same State, claiming lands under grants of different States, fall within federal cognizance and are the only instances in which the proposed Constitution directly contemplates the cognizance of disputes between the citizens of the same State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State tribunals would be unlikely to be unbiased in such cases; federal courts are proper to avoid local prejudgment and ties to State grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases involving foreign states, citizens, or subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend to cases between a State and the citizens thereof, and foreign States, citizens, or subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such matters relate peculiarly to national judicature and have been previously explained as belonging to federal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of Congress to make exceptions and regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court would have appellate jurisdiction 'with such EXCEPTIONS and under such REGULATIONS as the Congress shall make.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If particular inconveniences arise from enumeration of federal powers, national legislature has ample authority to make exceptions and prescribe regulations to obviate or remove these inconveniences; possibility of mischiefs is not a sufficient objection to a general principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: One supreme final court is desirable
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be one court of supreme and final jurisdiction; it is preferred that the ultimate decision of all causes rest in a distinct and independent body rather than as a branch of the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A separate Supreme Court prevents intermixture of powers and the tendency of legislatures (who make laws) to be biased in interpreting them; contrasts with practice in Britain and many States where highest judicature is a legislative branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of functions: judges vs legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: A body which had even a partial agency in passing bad laws could rarely be expected to temper and moderate them in the application; men who infringed the Constitution as legislators would be less disposed to repair the breach as judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports independent judiciary and tenure for judges, as legislative members lack the specialized qualifications and permanence for judicial functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure during good behavior for judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure of good behavior for judicial offices is recommended; permanence and qualifications of judges argue against placing ultimate judicial power in bodies chosen for limited periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent judges accumulate legal knowledge by long study; temporary legislators are unlikely to have such qualifications and are more prone to faction and defective information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution as standard of construction for laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution ought to be the standard of construction for the laws, and wherever there is an evident opposition, the laws ought to give place to the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine flows from the general theory of a limited constitution and is not peculiar to the federal plan; federal courts are not given a unique prerogative beyond what necessity of limited constitutions implies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislatures cannot reverse judicial sentences in particular cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature, without exceeding its province, cannot reverse a determination once made in a particular case; though it may prescribe a new rule for future cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither British nor State constitutions authorize revisal of judicial sentences by legislative act in particular cases; this principle applies equally to the proposed federal system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment as check on judicial usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutional check of the power of instituting impeachments in one part of the legislative body, and determining upon them in the other, gives the legislature a complete security against judicial usurpations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the legislature can degrade judges by impeachment, there is little danger that judges would hazard united legislative resentment by systematic usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to constitute inferior courts to avoid Supreme Court overload
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of constituting inferior courts is calculated to obviate the necessity of having recourse to the Supreme Court in every case of federal cognizance; to enable the national government to institute or authorize, in each State or district, a tribunal competent to determination of national matters within its limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power allows creation of local federal tribunals or districts and is essential to practical administration of justice and to circumscribing appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for not confiding original federal cognizance solely to State courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Although State courts might be fit and competent, there are reasons against confiding original federal causes solely to them: local spirit may disqualify local tribunals, and some State courts (where judges hold offices during pleasure or year-to-year) are too little independent for inflexible execution of national laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If State courts were made original judges in federal causes, there would be a commensurate necessity for wide appeal rights; confidence in subordinate tribunals should determine the ease or difficulty of appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction both as to law and fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court shall possess appellate jurisdiction both as to law and FACT, subject to such exceptions and regulations as the national legislature may prescribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate jurisdiction covers review of proceedings either as to law or fact; 'appellate' in abstract denotes power to review one tribunal's proceedings and may be exercised with or without juries as legislative provision dictates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-examination of facts decided by juries may be regulated
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-examination of a fact once ascertained by a jury need not be permitted in the Supreme Court, but the same court may take cognizance of facts as they appear on the record and pronounce the law arising upon them; re-examination may be effected by remanding for a second trial or directing an issue out of the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves trial by jury in practice; appellate review can be designed to avoid abolishing jury trials while allowing necessary fact-review in certain civil-law-type cases (e.g., prize causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction of State courts by default
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts will retain the jurisdiction they now have unless it appears to be taken away in one of three modes (express grant of exclusive authority to Union; grant to Union with prohibition to States; grant to Union incompatible with State exercise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rule, state courts take cognizance of causes arising under federal laws where not expressly excluded; national and state systems are parts of one whole and state courts are natural auxiliaries to federal law execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal lies from state tribunals to Supreme Court
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal would certainly lie from the state tribunals to the Supreme Court of the United States because the Constitution gives appellate jurisdiction to the Supreme Court in all enumerated cases of federal cognizance without confining its operation to inferior federal courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects of appeal are the classes of cases, not the tribunals from which they come; without such appeals the judiciary authority of the Union might be eluded by plaintiffs selecting state tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical districting and circuit plan for inferior courts
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be expedient to divide the United States into four or five or half a dozen districts and to institute a federal court in each district, in lieu of one in every State, with judges of these courts aided by state judges holding circuits for trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This plan would administer justice with ease and dispatch and allow appeals to be safely circumscribed within a narrow compass.
